question: The Swiss judiciary has for the second time warned a Spanish judge about the political nature of his investigation in a case relating to Catalan independence that involves a Member of the European Parliament.

The Swiss judges warn that they will not cooperate with the Spanish justice system if it does not address the weak evidence supporting the accusation of terrorism, and the arbitrary classification of acts covered by freedom of expression, assembly and demonstration or equivalent to much more specific and minor offences.

Moreover, they highlight the obvious interference of the investigation in decisions of the legislative authorities. These warnings and disqualifications come in addition to those in other EU Member States on the same issue regarding senior members of Spain’s judicial system. 1.
Does the Commission consider that the repetition of such events could indicate a systemic problem in the way in which certain minorities are dealt with in Spanish courts?
Is the Commission going to include this issue in its next EU Rule of Law Report by at least listening actively to those affected by this systemic behaviour?
answer: As reflected in the Commission’s 2022 and 2023 Rule of Law Reports (1), according to European standards, while courts are not immune to criticism and scrutiny, the judiciary must enjoy public confidence to be successful in view of its special role in society.

This is particularly important in relation to statements by members of the legislative and the executive branches, as all powers of the State must foster and protect the trust of the general public in constitutional institutions including the judiciary.

Switzerland is a party to a number of multilateral conventions on the basis of which mutual legal assistance can be provided, including the Council of Europe Convention on Mutual Assistance in Criminal Matters (2) and its Second Additional Protocol (3), the Convention Implementing the Schengen Agreement (4) and the Council of Europe Convention on Cybercrime (Budapest Convention) (5).
Furthermore, requests can also be made on the basis of the principle of reciprocity (6).
